items.prose: The course's rule on one date: listed, at least 60 days of trading, and a 60-day average £ volume of at least £5m.
items.question: How many of these five shares are in the universe?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply all three tests to each share.

byKey.q: Q has £50m a day but only 40 days of trading.
byKey.all: Q is too new, R is not listed and T is below £5m.

explain.text: P passes and so does S, at £5.20m. Q is too new, R has delisted and T trades £4.10m a day.

items.prose: A share closed at £240 before a four-for-one split. Today it closes at £63.
items.question: What is the split-adjusted pre-split close, in £?

feedback.correct: £60: the share is up 5% since then, in today's shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the earlier close by the split ratio.

byKey.times: You multiplied. Earlier closes are divided by the ratio.
byKey.half: You divided by 2. A four-for-one split divides by 4.

explain.text: Each old share became four new ones, so £240 then is £60 in today's shares. Against £63 now, the share rose 5%.

items.prose: A universe of 300 shares loses 6 a year to delisting, with an average last-day return of −80%.
items.question: About how much does a study on survivors only overstate the equal-weighted mean return, in % a year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the deaths per share per year by the average loss.

byKey.ratio: That is $k/N$ alone. Multiply by the 80% loss.

explain.text: Two per cent of the universe dies each year with an 80% loss, so dropping them adds about $0.02 \times 0.8 = 1.6\%$ a year.

items.prose: After day $t$ a share returns +1%, −2% and +3%.
items.question: What is its three-day forward return on row $t$, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compound the three growth factors.

byKey.sum: You added the returns. Over time they compound.

explain.text: $1.01 \times 0.98 \times 1.03 = 1.019494$, so 1.95%. Adding gives 2.00%, close but wrong.

items.prose: A share listed on 3 March 2021 and died on 9 September 2022. Another listed in 2019 and is listed today. A third died in 2020.
items.question: Which belong in a point-in-time universe on 1 June 2021, if each passes the £5m filter? Select all that apply.

options.why: It stopped trading in 2020, so nobody could hold it in June 2021.

feedback.correct: Both shares that traded on that date.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which shares were listed on 1 June 2021, with 60 days of trading.

explain.text: On 1 June 2021 the March listing has about 63 trading days, so it passes. Its 2022 death does not matter in 2021. The 2020 death is long gone.

items.prose: A share closes at £150. The next day it splits two for one, pays a dividend of £0.75 per new share, and closes at £74.25.
items.question: What is that day's total return, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by the split ratio and add the dividend per new share.

byKey.nodiv: You forgot the dividend: two shares also pay £1.50 in cash.
byKey.raw: That is the raw-close change. The holder has two shares.

explain.text: Two new shares at £74.25 plus £0.75 cash each make £150, the value held before. The return is 0, whatever the raw close says.

items.prose: `L` is a frame of daily log returns.
items.question: Which line gives the five-day forward log return on row $t$, days $t + 1$ to $t + 5$?

options.why: Row $t$ then covers days $t$ to $t + 4$, including day $t$, which the signal also uses.
That is the past five days, ending on $t$: a signal, not a forward return.
That window ends on day $t + 1$ and starts on $t - 3$: mostly the past.

feedback.correct: The window ending on $t + 5$, moved back to row $t$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the days row $t$ covers in each line.

explain.text: `rolling(5)` on row $t + 5$ covers $t + 1$ to $t + 5$; `shift(-5)` moves it to row $t$. One row less and day $t$ is inside the window.

items.prose: Edge case. On row $t$ a study holds three shares equally for five days. X returns +3% and Y −1% over the window. Z returns +2% and then −60% on its last day, and has no later returns.
items.question: What is the portfolio's five-day forward return, in %?

feedback.correct: −19.07%: Z's death is inside the window.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compound Z's two days, then average the three forward returns.

byKey.drop: You dropped Z because its window has NaN. Its holder still lost 59.2%.
byKey.last: You used −60% for Z. It gained 2% first: $1.02 \times 0.40 - 1 = -0.592$.

explain.text: Z's forward return compounds to its death: $1.02 \times 0.40 - 1 = -0.592$. Averaged with +3% and −1% it gives −19.07%. Dropping Z would report +1%.

items.prose: A share traded £1m a day for a long time, then £10m a day from day 1 of a new contract. The rule uses the trailing 60-day mean, today included, and needs at least £5m.
items.question: On which day at £10m does the share first pass the filter?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After $k$ days at £10m the mean is $(60 - k + 10k)/60$.

byKey.thirty: Half the window at £10m gives £5.5m, already above £5m. It passes earlier.

explain.text: After $k$ days the mean is $(60 + 9k)/60$, which reaches 5 at $k = 26.7$. Day 27 is the first whole day above £5m. A whole-sample mean would have admitted the share long before.
